questions.question: What motivated you to go on exchange? (pick the most important one) *
questions.answer: Explore new cultures

questions.question: Which aspects were crucial to choosing your study destination? *
questions.answer: NUS has a reputation for being a good uni, and their philosophy department is analytic, which was important to me. Furthermore, I wanted to go somewhere really different to Denmark. Since I don't speak a third language, though, it had to be somewhere with undergrad courses in English. Singapore perfectly fit the bill!

questions.question: How would you rate your overall study abroad experience? *
Additional comments:
How easy was it to find the information you needed to know upon arrival? *
questions.answer: Pretty easy. The Singaporean system is quite bureaucratic, but there are a lot of people ready to help, and in my experience you can often send a question to an administrative body and receive a reply the next day at the latest. That is really a huge help when trying to navigate the jungle of visas, accommodation, course enrollment etc.

questions.question: What assistance, if any, did you receive when you arrived at your study destination? *
questions.answer: I got fairly elaborate guides via email about where I had to go and when, and was quite lucky with all of the practical and logistical stuff regarding my arrival. However, perhaps my batch of exchangers were bigger than usual - it seemed NUS struggled with too few resources to guide us all properly in the beginning. I know for example that many couldn't get an appointment to finish their student visa because NUS simply had too few slots. And many didn't get student accommonation, which forced them out to the expensive and competitive private housing market. I sensed that these things made arrival quite stressful for the unlucky ones.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the orientation and assistance available to students at your host institution upon arrival? *
Additional comments
How did you find housing? *
questions.answer: I found housing through my host institution

questions.question: Did you live on campus or off campus? *
questions.answer: On campus

questions.question: What options were available for on campus housing? *
questions.answer: There are residential colleges with meal plans and a lot of social activities, and accommodation which I gather is less social and more of just a room on campus. Don't know too much about the latter, though.

questions.question: What options were available for meal plans or cooking facilities? *
questions.answer: If you live in a residential college (RC4 or CAPT, for example) the meal plan is obligatory. There are also kitchens for light cooking, but they are dirty and not very well-equipped. The meal plan is great, though, and an awesome way to meet people. If you get accommodation without a meal plan, I got the sense that most people use the canteens on campus a lot, where you can get good and varied meals for every taste for 4USD or less. I think they also have kitchens for light cooking, but they don't have a stove, for instance.

questions.question: What should future exchange students know about living in on campus housing? *
questions.answer: I stayed at RC4 and have been so happy about it. Most of my friends I met there, and you absolutely live like royalty: No cooking, no cleaning, no grocery shopping. Everything is taken care of for you, and I found the food in the dining hall quite decent, even as vegetarian. And living on campus has been super convenient. I should mention, though, that I think the residential colleges (RC4 and CAPT) are the nicest residences. My impression is that places like PGPR and UTown are more of just a place to sleep - less of a community. Still convenient and cheaper options, though. However, many didn't get student accommodation via NUS, and I think they struggled. The private market here is expensive, and you can end up either living very far from campus with a long commute or have to share a room with 1-3 other people in a poorly kept residence.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the housing available to students? *
Additional comments:
How easy did you find the registration process at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
Please describe the registration process at your host institution *
questions.answer: Again, I was very lucky: I got all of my top-priority courses right off the bat because I'm in humanities where courses are less competed for. For me, registration was totally painless. But my friends in computer science and economics didn't secure the required amount of modules in the first round, so it was unclear if they could go at all, and because they had to wait for second round of course registration, they missed the deadline for on-campus housing applications. This was super stressful for them and not very well-organized by NUS, I think.

questions.question: What kind of help was available? *
questions.answer: You can email the international office or whichever office is in charge of the area you need help with, and they will be very helpful in guiding you through the formal processes.

questions.question: How successful were you in registering for the classes you wanted? *
questions.answer: Succesful. I got four of top five priorities - the last course I wanted wasn't offered this semester.

questions.question: What advice would you offer to future exchange students about registration at your host institution? *
questions.answer:
I really don't know how to make the process easier. I know I had a very much easier time because I applied for courses without that much competition (third year philosophy courses, a decision theory module and a module in global health). But I'm not sure strategizing helps too much, because it's hard to predict which courses are very sought after. Check out the opportunities on
nusmods.com
and see what strikes your interest. Oh yeah, and check out the professor online if you can before you choose. In my experience, having a good professor is (here as anywhere else) almost as important to your final learning outcome than the course content itself.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the academic programme at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
Were you a BA or MA student at UCPH when you were on exchange? *
questions.answer: BA

questions.question: Please elaborate on the level of courses *
questions.answer: It varied a lot. My philosophy modules (level 3000) were extremely good - small classes of 6-10 people, very competent professors and motivated students. I have had some of the best teaching I have ever experienced here. And the level was high, significantly higher than in UCPH, I'd say. Readings were harder and the profs expected more of us. However, I have also had an introductory course meant for PPE students (level 3000) which was very poor. The professor was a bad teacher, students were unmotivated. This course was fairly easy.

questions.question: How did the style of teaching at your host institution compare with that of UCPH? *
questions.answer: In one module, introduction to global health, we had a lot of guest lectures from people working in different subfields. That was extremely nice. However, the assignments were hard for me to understand, simply because I had trouble getting the different format. We were asked to write 'reflections', and I never quite understood what the prof wanted for us. This module also had more group work than I'm used to. In philosophy, the style was pretty much the same as I'm used to: Prof at the whiteboard going over the assigned papers for the day and class discussion about any unclarities.

questions.question: How long were you on exchange? *
questions.answer: 1 semester

questions.question: Please list the courses you were enrolled in during your first semester. *
questions.answer: SPH2401 Introduction to global health, PE3101P Decision and social choice, PH3250 Quantification and modality, PH3245 Language and thought

questions.question: What specific courses would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer: If you are interested in philosophy, I recommend Language and Thought very much! It's a niche topic, but the professor I had (fall 2022) made it so engaging and fun.

What unexpected costs did you encounter? *
questions.answer: Well, I ended up spending a good amount traveling! Other than that, I don't think I've encountered any

questions.question: What items were more or less expensive than you expected? *
questions.answer: Public transport is very affordable! So are taxis (use Grab) if you carpool with someone. And so is food, at least when you eat in hawker centers, which I absolutely recommend. My housing (residential college on campus) was fairly affordable as well, considering it included 12 meals a week. And getting a prepaid sim card (e.g. Singtel) is a very easy and cheap solution for getting your phone online. Groceries are expensive, though! More so than in Denmark. I have not been cooking at all since I got here, so of course eating out is an expense. And note that if you don't get student housing, the private housing market is tough.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the non-academic opportunities (clubs, sports, etc.) at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
What kinds of cultural, athletic and social activities were available for students at your host institution? *
questions.answer: A lot of clubs and societies. Board game club, film club, music, dancing. Definitely something for everyone! The sports facilities here are great - olympic sized pool, climbing wall, gym etc. Sports clubs as well, which are quite high-level competitive from what I've heard.

questions.question: Which non -academic activities would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer: The film club! A screening of a lovely international masterpiece every Friday evening with discussion afterwards! Lovely space. I think the sports clubs are a good opportunity for people at a more advanced level - not really beginner-friendly, I think. But whatever you like, search it out here. It's really valuable to get to know local students and I think this is a good way to do so.

questions.question: What do you recommend other visiting students see or do on their weekends or holidays? *
questions.answer: Exchange students here travel like crazy! To Indonesia, Malaysia, Thailand, Vietnam, even Japan, Taiwan and South Korea! This is fun, but I think it is also valuable to stay in Singapore and build a more solid foundation here. A lot of museums are free, because exchangers count as 'local resident' when we have our student pass. Go to Little India and Chinatown and explore the cities within the citites. Go to Pulau Ubin and see the hornbills, and to Sungei Buloh and see the alligators.

questions.question: How easy was it to adjust to the local culture of your exchange site? *
questions.answer: Easy. Honestly, Singapore is just very westernized, and I was surprised by how little of a culture shock-factor it was. Everyone speaks English, infrastructure is super efficient, everything is available online.

questions.question: Do you have any tips for socializing with local students?
questions.answer: Join clubs and sports and just be open. Be that awkward person who asks people to lunch even though you don't know them well enough for that by Danish standards. It pays off!

questions.question: What, if any, cultural differences did you find particularly challenging? *
questions.answer: It can be a bit difficult to get close to Singaporean students. I guess they share some of the closed off-ness that we Scandinavians have, plus maybe some. So you don't necessarily get to know people very well through group work and the like, and it can take some stamina to get accepted into social circles, I think.

questions.question: What parts of the culture did you most appreciate? *
questions.answer: The international melting pot-vibe of Singapore. You can find foods from all regions, people from all places and backgrounds, and that's really nice. And I did find some local students who were very welcoming, invited me home to meet their parents and so on, which was so nice.

questions.question: What are the three most important things you would tell a UCPH student who is going to your host institution on exchange? *
questions.answer: Don't let yourself be scared off by the bureaucracy. Once you're here and have gotten the formalities fixed, it's really quite easy to navigate the systems, figure out exam schedules and so on and so forth. Be prepared to work hard academically. I've heard many different things from exchangers - some say it's easier than at their home uni, but in my experience, demands are quite high, and profs here expect you to take responsibility for your own understanding. And then - know that it'll take some work to make friends. Any exchange takes some getting out of your comfort zone, I suppose, and this is no exception. Don't expect to necessarily meet the love of your life (though I know some have!) or make friends that'll last a lifetime. After all, 4 months is a short time to get to know people. But you can count on plenty of fun encounters and lovely people to spend time with while it lasts!

questions.question: Is there any other information that you think might prove useful to future exchange students attending your host institution? *
questions.answer: A few quick things: Getting around campus is super easy with the free shuttle bus. Don't underestimate the heat: I applied for a room without AC because I generally like warmer weather and thought surely I could handle it. I wasn't prepared for the tropical humid heat and definitely would have slept a lot worse if I hadn't gotten a room with AC! There is a midterm recess week with no classes which is a good opportunity to travel. Singapore itself is a strange place: Lovely and green while at the same time filled with sky scrapers. But it's also very clean and orderly, it's illegal to demonstrate, chewing gum is banned because it makes a mess on the streets and public transport doesn't run after around 11pm to disencourage people to go out drinking. In that sense, it's an interesting place to be! And it's easy to settle in, not too much of a culture shock while being still very different from Denmark. All in all, I definitely recommend NUS.

questions.question: What was the most rewarding part of your exchange experience? *
questions.answer: Experiencing a completely different culture in Asia and meeting people here from all over the world. Also, the teaching has really been great. I have learned much more than I could've hoped for.

questions.question: What was the greatest challenge during the exchange? *
questions.answer: Honestly, it's been surprisingly easy. One thing I have struggled with is the exchanger FOMO. Everyone travels everywhere and it seems there is this expectation that you see all of Asia while you're here. I've spent a lot of time (too much time) making travel plans just because I felt I should, and that's a shame. I wish I could've found a better balance between traveling some and also just exploring Singapore, discovering what the local communities have to offer.

questions.question: Any other comments?
Do you agree to share your travel report with other fellow students? *
questions.answer: Yes
